tasks.title: Health messaging and public trust
tasks.instruction: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answers.

promptBlocks.label: Text 1
promptBlocks.text: Public health campaigns that rely on fear-based messaging are often defended on the grounds that they produce rapid behavioural change. Yet the evidence suggests that such campaigns can erode trust in the very authorities that issue them. When people are told that a common behaviour is lethal, and then observe that the predicted harm does not materialise for most, they may conclude that the warning was exaggerated. This breeds scepticism not only about the specific message but about future health advice from the same source. A more responsible approach would prioritise honest communication about uncertainty, even if it makes the message less dramatic. Trust, once lost, is far harder to rebuild than a campaign slogan.

promptBlocks.label: Text 2
promptBlocks.text: The demand that public health messages be perfectly honest about uncertainty is naive. People respond to clear, decisive guidance, not to nuanced caveats. During a crisis, the public needs to know what to do, not to be invited into a seminar on statistical probability. Over-qualifying a warning can lead to inaction, which costs lives. Moreover, the claim that fear-based messages erode trust assumes a passive, gullible public. In reality, citizens are capable of understanding that health authorities must sometimes act on incomplete information. The greater risk to trust is not a dramatic alert that turns out to be overstated, but a hesitant message that arrives too late to be useful.

tasks.title: Review of a health campaign documentary
tasks.instruction: Answer one of the following questions (2–4). Write 280–320 words in an appropriate style.
tasks.promptText: A specialist magazine for public health professionals is running a series of reviews of documentaries that examine the relationship between health messaging and public trust. You decide to submit a review of a recent documentary called 'The Persuasion Gap', which follows the design and public reception of a national vaccination campaign. In your review, evaluate how effectively the documentary captures the tension between persuasive messaging and honest communication, discuss whether it gives adequate attention to the perspectives of those who remained sceptical, and assess the overall value of the film for professionals planning future campaigns.

tasks.title: Report on public trust in health campaigns
tasks.instruction: Answer one of the following questions (2–4). Write 280–320 words in an appropriate style.
tasks.promptText: You are a consultant hired by the National Institute for Health Communication. The programme coordinator has asked you to write a report analysing the implications of a recent decline in public trust following a series of high-profile health campaigns that used strong fear appeals. In your report, analyse the main factors that contributed to the erosion of trust, assess the potential consequences for future public health initiatives if trust is not restored, and propose two concrete actions the institute could take to rebuild credibility while maintaining the effectiveness of its messaging.

tasks.title: Honesty in health messaging
tasks.instruction: Answer one of the following questions (2–4). Write 280–320 words in an appropriate style.
tasks.promptText: An English-language online magazine for international readers is publishing a series on 'The Ethics of Persuasion'. You have been contacted by an editor who is an English-speaking contact of yours. The editor asks you to write an article explaining your position on whether public health campaigns should prioritise honesty about uncertainty over the persuasive power of clear, decisive messages. In your article, explain your position on this question, describe one practical consequence of your view for how health authorities design campaigns, and suggest how communicators could balance the need for clarity with the responsibility to be truthful. End your article by requesting that the magazine arrange a follow-up online discussion with readers and health communication experts to explore the issue further.
